quote: Problem der 3 Körper 1.) eine feste 2.) zwei feste Bedingungen. 3.) Bedingungen aufstellen, dass sich die 3 Körper in einem Punkte treffen. Versuch der Annahme: $y=\sin(x^2+c^2)$
english: Three-body problem: 1.) one fixed, 2.) two fixed conditions. 3.) Set up conditions for the 3 bodies to meet at one point. Attempt with the assumption $y=\sin(x^2+c^2)$.
topic: A list of research topics and problems on binary forms, covariants, invariants, the principle of special position, and the three-body problem.

triage.modern_statement: Newtonian three-body problem: find conditions on the initial data (masses, positions, velocities) under which all three bodies collide at a single point, i.e. a triple collision or total collapse. The items '1.) one fixed, 2.) two fixed conditions' are too brief to pin down. They may refer to restricted versions where one or two bodies, or one or two conditions, are held fixed. The trial function y = sin(x^2 + c^2) was an ad hoc attempt and has no identifiable later use.
triage.answered_by: Weierstrass knew the key necessary condition by 1889 (letter to Mittag-Leffler): total collapse can only happen if the total angular momentum is zero. Karl F. Sundman proved it independently and published it about two decades later (1907–1912). In 1912 Sundman also showed that triple collisions are asymptotically central configurations (Euler collinear or Lagrange equilateral). Later work studied the structure of triple-collision orbits in detail, notably McGehee's blow-up of the triple collision (1974).

evidence.claim: Sundman–Weierstrass total collapse theorem: if the total angular momentum is non-zero, collapse cannot happen.
Weierstrass knew the result and communicated it to Mittag-Leffler in an 1889 letter. Sundman independently obtained and published a proof about two decades later.
Sundman showed there are no triple collisions in the three-body problem when angular momentum is non-zero. In 1912 he showed that triple collisions are asymptotically central configurations.

McGehee (1974) used an extension of spherical coordinates plus a time reparametrization to remove the triple-collision singularity from the flow. This 'blow-up' replaces the collision point with a manifold.

triage.why: Item 3 clearly asks for conditions under which the 3 bodies meet at one point. That is the classical question of triple collision (total collapse). Its central necessary condition, zero angular momentum, was known to Weierstrass (1889) and proved by Sundman (1907–1912). Sundman also described how bodies approach a triple collision. So the identifiable core of the note was answered, though not by Hilbert. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. Items 1 and 2 and the sine trial function are too brief to identify, which is why confidence is medium rather than high. Collision singularities, McGehee blow-up and triple-collision dynamics are still studied in celestial mechanics, as recent arXiv papers show. Still, the precise question in the note was settled about a century ago.
